episodes.title: Central Corneal Thickness: Pachymetry & IOP Correction for ODs
episodes.description:
Are you interpreting intraocular pressure without accounting for central corneal thickness? If so, you may be putting your glaucoma suspect patients at risk. In this episode of Focus Cast by Focuslinks.in, we break down one of the most clinically impactful yet underutilized concepts in optometric glaucoma care: pachymetry correction and how CCT fundamentally changes the way you read Goldmann applanation tonometry results.

We walk through the physiological basis of tonometric error, explaining why the Goldmann tonometer's assumed baseline of 520 microns creates real diagnostic blind spots across a population where corneal thickness varies dramatically. We then unpack the landmark Ocular Hypertension Treatment Study (OHTS) and its defining finding: that a CCT below 555 microns carries a three-fold increased risk of conversion to primary open-angle glaucoma, independent of IOP, cup-to-disc ratio, and visual field status.

From there, we get practical. You will learn how to apply pachymetry-based IOP correction formulas chairside, what to look for on slit lamp, gonioscopy, OCT, and fundus examination, how to build a differential diagnosis around CCT data, and how to use the OHTS risk framework to decide between initiating topical therapy, monitoring, or referring to a glaucoma specialist.

This episode is designed exclusively for licensed optometrists, optometry residents, and clinical eye care practitioners who want evidence-based, immediately applicable clinical guidance. If you are serious about delivering accurate glaucoma risk assessments, this is essential listening.

Subscribe to Focus Cast and visit Focuslinks.in for more clinically focused content built specifically for eye care professionals.

episodes.content:
Welcome to Focus Cast by Focuslinks dot in, the podcast built for eye care professionals who want sharp, clinically relevant insights delivered in a format that fits your busy schedule. Whether you are between patients, on your commute, or winding down after a long clinic day, you are in the right place. Today we are diving deep into something that every optometrist encounters regularly but that does not always get the nuanced attention it deserves. We are talking about central corneal thickness, pachymetry correction, and how this single measurement can completely change the way you interpret intraocular pressure and make treatment decisions for your glaucoma suspects. So let us get into it.

Here is a scenario that probably sounds familiar. You have a patient sitting in your chair. Forty-eight years old, no family history of glaucoma, healthy optic nerves, normal visual fields. But their IOP is sitting at twenty-four millimeters of mercury on Goldmann applanation tonometry. You are thinking, do I treat this person? Do I refer? Do I watch and wait? And then you pull up their pachymetry reading. Five hundred and forty microns. Suddenly, that twenty-four does not look quite the same as it did thirty seconds ago. That is the power of understanding central corneal thickness in your clinical workflow, and that is exactly what we are unpacking today.

Let us start with the basics, because even if you have been practicing for years, it is worth grounding ourselves in the physiology before we get into the clinical decision-making. The Goldmann applanation tonometer, which remains the gold standard for IOP measurement in clinical practice, was calibrated based on an assumed central corneal thickness of five hundred and twenty microns. That is the number the instrument was designed around. But here is the thing. Corneal thickness varies significantly across the population. Studies show that CCT can range anywhere from below four hundred and fifty microns to well above six hundred microns in otherwise healthy eyes. That is a massive range, and it has real consequences for how accurately Goldmann tonometry reflects true intraocular pressure.

When the cornea is thicker than that assumed five hundred and twenty micron baseline, the tonometer has to work harder to applanate the corneal surface. This means it overestimates the true IOP. Conversely, when the cornea is thinner than average, the tonometer underestimates the true IOP. So a patient with a very thin cornea, say four hundred and eighty microns, might have a Goldmann reading of eighteen millimeters of mercury, which looks perfectly normal, but their actual IOP could be significantly higher. That is a patient who could be silently progressing toward glaucomatous damage while you are reassuring them that everything looks fine. That is the clinical danger here, and it is why pachymetry is not optional in a comprehensive glaucoma evaluation.

Now let us talk about the landmark study that really put this issue on the map for the optometric and ophthalmologic community. The Ocular Hypertension Treatment Study, commonly known as OHTS, was a pivotal multicenter randomized clinical trial that followed over fifteen hundred patients with elevated IOP but no glaucomatous damage. The study identified several key risk factors for conversion from ocular hypertension to primary open-angle glaucoma. And one of the most significant findings, one that genuinely surprised many clinicians at the time, was that central corneal thickness was a powerful independent predictor of glaucoma development. Patients with thinner corneas had a substantially higher risk of converting to glaucoma, even after controlling for IOP, age, cup-to-disc ratio, and visual field status.

The OHTS established that a CCT below five hundred and fifty-five microns was associated with a three-fold increase in the risk of developing glaucoma compared to patients with thicker corneas. That is not a subtle finding. That is a clinically significant, practice-changing result. And the study used a threshold of twenty-four millimeters of mercury as the upper boundary for defining ocular hypertension in their cohort. So when you are sitting with a patient whose IOP is hovering around that twenty-four threshold, knowing their CCT is not just helpful, it is essential for accurate risk stratification.

Let us move into the practical correction side of things, because this is where chairside decision-making really comes into play. There are several correction formulas and nomograms that have been proposed over the years to adjust Goldmann IOP readings based on CCT. The most commonly referenced correction factor suggests that for every ten microns of corneal thickness above or below the five hundred and twenty micron baseline, you adjust the IOP by approximately one to two millimeters of mercury. So if your patient has a CCT of five hundred and seventy microns, which is fifty microns above baseline, you might subtract somewhere between two and a half to five millimeters of mercury from their Goldmann reading to get a more accurate estimate of true IOP. And if their CCT is four hundred and seventy microns, fifty microns below baseline, you would add that correction back in.

Now, I want to be clear here. These correction formulas are estimates, not exact science. The relationship between corneal thickness and tonometric error is not perfectly linear, and it is influenced by other corneal biomechanical properties like corneal hysteresis and corneal resistance factor. Instruments like the Ocular Response Analyzer and the Corvis ST attempt to account for these biomechanical variables and give you a more biomechanically corrected IOP. If you have access to these instruments, they add another layer of precision to your assessment. But even without them, applying a thoughtful pachymetry-based correction to your Goldmann readings is far better than ignoring CCT entirely.

Let us talk about clinical presentation and what you are looking for in the exam. Your glaucoma suspect or ocular hypertension patient typically presents without symptoms. That is the insidious nature of this disease. They are not coming in complaining of vision loss. They are coming in for their routine comprehensive exam, and you are the one who catches the elevated IOP on tonometry. Your slit lamp examination should be thorough. You are looking at the anterior segment for any secondary causes of elevated IOP, things like pseudoexfoliation material on the anterior lens capsule or pupillary margin, pigment dispersion with Krukenberg spindle on the corneal endothelium, or signs of prior uveitis that might indicate a secondary glaucoma mechanism. Gonioscopy is critical. You need to know whether the angle is open or closed before you can accurately classify what you are dealing with.

On fundus examination, you are carefully evaluating the optic nerve head. You are looking at the cup-to-disc ratio, the neuroretinal rim tissue, the presence of any disc hemorrhages, and the peripapillary retinal nerve fiber layer. A vertical cup-to-disc ratio greater than point six, asymmetry between the two eyes of more than point two, inferior or superior notching of the rim, or any disc hemorrhage should raise your index of suspicion significantly. OCT of the retinal nerve fiber layer and ganglion cell complex gives you objective structural data that complements your clinical impression. Baseline OCT imaging is essential in any patient you are monitoring for glaucoma risk, because it gives you a reference point for detecting future progression.

Visual field testing with standard automated perimetry is your functional assessment. In early glaucoma suspects, the visual field may be entirely normal, which is why structural assessment with OCT is so valuable. Glaucomatous structural changes often precede detectable functional loss by years. So do not wait for a field defect to take action.

Now let us bring this all together with a differential diagnosis framework. When you have a patient with elevated IOP, your differential includes primary open-angle glaucoma, ocular hypertension, normal tension glaucoma in patients with IOP that appears normal but may be falsely low due to thin corneas, pseudoexfoliation glaucoma, pigmentary glaucoma, and angle-closure mechanisms. CCT measurement helps you refine this differential. A patient with a very thin cornea and an IOP of twenty-one might actually have a true IOP of twenty-five or twenty-six, which changes your entire risk assessment. A patient with a very thick cornea and an IOP of twenty-six might have a true IOP closer to twenty-two, which is far less concerning.

For management and referral decisions, the OHTS data gives us a useful framework. Patients with IOP between twenty-four and thirty-two millimeters of mercury, no glaucomatous optic nerve damage, and no visual field loss are candidates for either treatment or observation depending on their overall risk profile. CCT is a major input into that risk calculation. A patient with thin corneas, a large cup-to-disc ratio, older age, and higher IOP has a substantially elevated five-year risk of conversion and warrants either initiation of topical IOP-lowering therapy or prompt referral to a glaucoma specialist. A patient with thick corneas, a modest cup-to-disc ratio, and borderline IOP may be safely monitored with close follow-up, repeat tonometry, serial OCT, and visual fields every six to twelve months.

When you do refer, make sure your referral is complete. Send the glaucoma specialist your pachymetry measurements, your gonioscopy findings, your OCT data, your visual field results, and your corrected IOP estimates. A well-documented referral not only helps the specialist, it reflects the quality of your clinical thinking and builds your professional reputation.

One final thought before we wrap up. Pachymetry is a quick, non-invasive measurement that takes less than a minute to perform. There is no reason it should not be part of every glaucoma evaluation you do. If you are not routinely measuring CCT in your ocular hypertension and glaucoma suspect patients, today is the day to change that. The OHTS data is clear. The clinical logic is sound. And your patients deserve the most accurate risk assessment you can provide.

Central corneal thickness is not just a number. It is a lens through which you interpret everything else. It changes your IOP, it changes your risk stratification, and it changes your management decisions. Master this concept, apply it consistently, and you will be a sharper, more confident clinician for every glaucoma patient who walks through your door.

Thank you so much for spending part of your day with Focus Cast. If you found this episode valuable, share it with a colleague, leave a review, and keep the conversation going. For more clinically focused content built specifically for optometrists and eye care professionals, visit Focus Cast at Focuslinks dot in. Until next time, keep your clinical thinking sharp and your patients in clear focus.

episodes.title: Gonioscopy & Glaucoma: Open-Angle vs Angle-Closure Explained
episodes.description:
Can you confidently classify a glaucoma suspect's angle at the slit lamp — and does your management change based on what you find? In this clinical episode of Focus Cast by Focuslinks.in, we break down one of the most critical distinctions in glaucoma care: the gonioscopic divide between open-angle and angle-closure disease.

Designed exclusively for optometrists, residents, and eye care clinicians, this episode walks you through the anterior chamber angle landmarks — ciliary body band, scleral spur, trabecular meshwork, and Schwalbe's line — and how the Shaffer grading system gives you a standardized framework for documentation and decision-making. We cover the clinical profiles of primary open-angle glaucoma versus primary angle-closure suspects, the Van Herick technique as your pre-gonioscopy screening tool, and the crucial difference between appositional and synechial closure on indentation gonioscopy.

You will also learn how to identify secondary glaucoma mechanisms including pigment dispersion syndrome, pseudoexfoliation, and neovascular glaucoma — all through the gonioscopic lens. From first-line prostaglandin analog therapy in open-angle disease to laser peripheral iridotomy in angle-closure, and from plateau iris management to acute angle-closure crisis protocols, this episode delivers evidence-based, chairside-ready guidance you can apply immediately.

Whether you are refining your gonioscopy technique or sharpening your referral thresholds, this episode gives you the clinical clarity to protect your patients' vision at every stage of glaucoma management.

Listen now and visit Focuslinks.in for more episodes and clinical resources built specifically for eye care professionals.

---
episodes.content:
Welcome to Focus Cast by Focuslinks dot in, the podcast built for eye care professionals who want sharp clinical thinking delivered straight to their ears. I'm glad you're here, and today we are diving into one of the most consequential distinctions in all of glaucoma management. The divide between open-angle and angle-closure glaucoma. And more specifically, why gonioscopy is the one exam you simply cannot skip when you are sitting across from a glaucoma suspect.

So let's set the scene. You have a patient in your chair. Their IOP is elevated. Maybe it's 24 in one eye, 26 in the other. The optic nerve looks a little suspicious, perhaps a cup-to-disc ratio of 0.7 with some inferior rim thinning. Your OCT shows borderline retinal nerve fiber layer loss in the inferior quadrant. Everything is pointing toward glaucoma. But here is the question that changes everything. What is the angle doing? Because if you do not know the answer to that question, you do not actually know what you are treating. And that distinction, open versus closed, is going to determine your entire management pathway.

Let's start with the anatomy, because understanding the angle is the foundation of everything we are about to discuss. The anterior chamber angle is the drainage structure of the eye. It sits at the junction of the cornea and the iris, and it houses the trabecular meshwork, which is the primary outflow pathway for aqueous humor. When we perform gonioscopy, we are essentially looking into this hidden recess using a mirrored contact lens to redirect our line of sight around the limbus. The landmarks we are identifying, from posterior to anterior, are the ciliary body band, the scleral spur, the trabecular meshwork, Schwalbe's line, and the cornea. That sequence, ciliary body, spur, meshwork, Schwalbe's, is your roadmap. And the Shaffer grading system gives us a standardized language to describe what we see. A grade four angle is wide open, about 35 to 45 degrees. A grade three is open, no risk of closure. A grade two is moderately narrow, closure is possible. A grade one is very narrow, closure is probable. And a grade zero means the angle is closed, with the iris touching the trabecular meshwork.

Now here is where clinical judgment becomes critical. A patient with primary open-angle glaucoma has a structurally open angle. The trabecular meshwork is visible, the drainage pathway is anatomically accessible, but it is functionally impaired. The resistance to outflow is increased at the level of the trabecular meshwork itself, and sometimes at the level of Schlemm's canal. The IOP rises gradually, the damage is insidious, and patients are often completely asymptomatic until significant visual field loss has occurred. This is the classic silent thief presentation that we talk about so often in glaucoma education.

Angle-closure, on the other hand, is a mechanically different disease. The iris physically obstructs the trabecular meshwork, either intermittently or permanently. And the subtypes matter here. Primary angle-closure suspect is when the angle is narrow but there is no peripheral anterior synechiae, no elevated IOP, and no glaucomatous damage. Primary angle-closure is when you have a narrow angle with either elevated IOP or peripheral anterior synechiae. And primary angle-closure glaucoma is when you have all of that plus optic nerve damage and visual field loss. Understanding where your patient sits on that spectrum changes your urgency and your treatment plan dramatically.

Let's talk about clinical presentation, because these two conditions can look deceptively similar on the surface. Both can present with elevated IOP. Both can show optic nerve cupping and RNFL thinning on OCT. Both can produce visual field defects that follow the arcuate pattern. But the history and the demographics often give you early clues. Open-angle glaucoma tends to affect older patients, is more prevalent in African American populations, and has a strong hereditary component. Angle-closure, by contrast, is more common in patients of East Asian descent, in women, in hyperopes, and in older patients with increasing lens thickness. That hyperopic patient in their sixties with a shallow anterior chamber and a crowded anterior segment, that is your angle-closure profile. And when they come in complaining of occasional blurry vision in dim lighting, or halos around lights at night, those are the intermittent angle-closure episodes that you need to take seriously.

The slit lamp examination gives you your first clues before you even pick up the gonio lens. Look at the anterior chamber depth. Use the Van Herick technique. If the peripheral anterior chamber depth is less than one quarter of the corneal thickness, you are looking at a potentially narrow angle. That is your signal to proceed with gonioscopy. Also look for iris configuration. A convex iris bowing forward, that is classic pupillary block. Look for pseudoexfoliation material on the lens capsule or pupillary margin, because pseudoexfoliation syndrome can drive both open-angle and angle-closure mechanisms. And always dilate carefully in these patients, because dilation in a narrow angle can precipitate acute closure.

Now let's talk about gonioscopy itself, because this is the skill that separates a thorough glaucoma workup from an incomplete one. There are two main lens types. The Goldmann single-mirror lens requires the patient to look in the direction of the mirror to view each quadrant. The Zeiss four-mirror lens allows you to view all four quadrants without repositioning, and it is particularly useful for indentation gonioscopy. And indentation gonioscopy is something every practitioner managing glaucoma suspects should be performing. When you apply gentle pressure with the Zeiss lens, you push aqueous into the angle and force the iris posteriorly. If the angle opens with indentation, the closure is appositional, meaning the iris is just resting against the meshwork without adhesion. If the angle does not open, you have synechial closure, meaning peripheral anterior synechiae have formed and the angle is permanently compromised in that region. That distinction is clinically enormous. Appositional closure can often be reversed with laser peripheral iridotomy. Synechial closure represents irreversible structural damage to the drainage pathway.

When you are at the slit lamp performing gonioscopy, use a narrow beam, keep the room dim, and avoid shining light directly through the pupil, because that will constrict the pupil and artificially open the angle, giving you a falsely reassuring view. Document your findings by quadrant. Note the most posterior structure visible in each quadrant. Note the presence or absence of peripheral anterior synechiae. Note any neovascularization of the angle, which would point you toward neovascular glaucoma. Note any pigment deposition on the trabecular meshwork, which can indicate pigment dispersion syndrome or pseudoexfoliation. These secondary causes of glaucoma have their own management nuances, and gonioscopy is how you find them.

Let's move into differential diagnosis and chairside decision-making, because this is where the rubber meets the road. You have done your gonioscopy. You have your angle grade. Now what? If the angle is open and the IOP is elevated with optic nerve changes, you are managing primary open-angle glaucoma or a suspect. Your first-line treatment is typically a prostaglandin analog, something like latanoprost or bimatoprost, dosed once nightly. These drugs work by increasing uveoscleral outflow and are highly effective in open-angle disease. You will monitor with serial visual fields, OCT of the RNFL and ganglion cell complex, and IOP measurements at multiple times of day to capture diurnal variation.

If the angle is narrow and you are seeing elevated IOP or synechiae, your management shifts significantly. Laser peripheral iridotomy is the cornerstone of angle-closure management. It creates an alternative pathway for aqueous to flow from the posterior chamber to the anterior chamber, relieving pupillary block and allowing the iris to fall back and open the angle. After LPI, you repeat gonioscopy to assess whether the angle has opened. If it has, and IOP normalizes, you may not need additional medication. If the angle remains narrow despite a patent iridotomy, you may be dealing with plateau iris configuration, where the ciliary processes are anteriorly rotated and physically push the peripheral iris forward. These patients may need laser iridoplasty or ongoing miotic therapy.

For acute angle-closure crisis, which is a true ocular emergency, the presentation is unmistakable. Severe eye pain, headache, nausea, vomiting, a rock-hard eye, corneal edema, a mid-dilated fixed pupil, and a dramatically elevated IOP, often above 40 or even 50 millimeters of mercury. This patient needs immediate intervention. You are reaching for topical beta-blockers, alpha agonists, carbonic anhydrase inhibitors, and potentially oral acetazolamide to break the attack medically while arranging urgent referral for laser or surgical intervention. Do not send this patient home. Do not wait until tomorrow. This is the scenario where delay costs vision.

Referral thresholds are something every optometrist needs to have clearly defined in their practice. Any patient with confirmed angle-closure glaucoma, any patient with acute angle-closure, any patient with progressive glaucomatous damage despite maximum tolerated medical therapy, and any patient where you suspect secondary glaucoma from neovascularization, trauma, or uveitis, all of these warrant prompt referral to a glaucoma specialist. Your role in co-management is equally important. You are often the first to identify these patients, and your thorough documentation, your gonioscopy findings, your OCT data, your visual field results, all of that becomes the foundation of the specialist's treatment plan.

Here is the takeaway I want you to carry into your next clinic day. Gonioscopy is not optional in a glaucoma workup. It is not a specialty procedure reserved for glaucoma subspecialists. It is a fundamental clinical skill that belongs in every optometric practice that manages glaucoma suspects. The angle tells you the mechanism of disease. The mechanism determines the treatment. And the treatment determines whether your patient keeps their vision. That is the gonioscopic divide, and it is one worth crossing every single time.

Thank you so much for spending this time with me today. If you found this episode clinically useful, share it with a colleague, a resident, or anyone in your practice who is building their glaucoma skills. We will be back with more evidence-based, practice-ready content designed specifically for eye care professionals like you. Visit Focus Cast at Focuslinks dot in for more episodes, resources, and clinical tools. Until next time, keep examining carefully, keep questioning what you see, and keep protecting the vision of every patient who sits in your chair.
